newsitem.title: UK: Dollar hit by FOMC decision, braces for more pain.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hit by FOMC decision, braces for more pain.

text.p: The dollar was frail in morning Europe, smarting from the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision to hold interest rates unchanged and bracing for further losses.

The policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) signalled no policy change after Tuesday's meeting, catching out a market which had priced in a 25 basis-point rise in the federal funds target rate.
"The Fed's taking a risk and the dollar's vulnerable to any sort of strong data or any pick-up in inflation," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ in London.
The dollar was quoted at 1.5062/68 marks by 0731 GMT, some way below late Tuesday's European level of 1.5125/30 although off a New York low of 1.5000.
Dollar/yen was more resilient, turning around an overnight dive to 108.95 to trade at 109.72/77, barely changed from its previous close in Europe.

The Fed's inaction had many market watchers speculating it could be "behind the curve" on inflation, and concerned that a reluctance to hike interest rates ahead of the U.S. elections had influenced its decision. That threw the focus onto the FOMC's next meeting on November 13.

Some also said Tuesday's meeting had lasted longer than usual, suggesting that there was a split over whether or not to change policy and so increasing the risk of a November rate hike if there was no further confirmation of economic slowdown.
Dealers said the dollar looked fragile after its inability to recoup its overnight losses against the mark.

"It's struggling a bit. A lot of people came in and believed it was the thing to do to buy the dollar for a rebound, but it doesn't look that healthy," said Peter Heath, senior dealer at Merita Bank here. He saw the upside blocked at around 1.5075, with a re-test of overnight lows possible.
Bids should protect the downside below 1.50 marks for now, however, Heath said. "I think the range has moved from 1.5120-70 to 1.5020-70," he added.

Some feared dollar/mark could probe even lower. Chase Investment Bank saw 1.4975 as the first target, with potential for a test of lows seen this summer -- when the dollar plunged as far as 1.4635 -- if that level was broken.
"We see the (Fed) decision as fairly unambiguously dollar negative," Chase said in its daily market brief.
All eyes will now be on U.S. data releases for confirmation that the economy is indeed decelerating, analysts said.
Today sees the release of U.S. existing home sales for August at 1400 GMT, although the market is more interested in Thursday's durable goods figures and Friday's GDP.
The really big one is the October 4 release of this month's U.S. non-farm payrolls, an indicator which has wreaked havoc on the markets in the past.
"I think the economy will slow down but I believe the risks are asymmetric," said IBJ's Edmonds. "If anything we're going to see inflation pick up given the tightness in the labour market."
Analysts warned that the dollar remained at risk if data indeed showed the U.S. economy losing momentum.

"As incoming data provides further evidence that the economy is decelerating, starting with durable goods tomorrow, the market will need to reconsider whether the Fed will still tighten this year," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell here.
"Such a reassessment could yet exert greater pressure on the dollar," he added.
All the same, analysts said the U.S. unit should claw some near-term support from the meeting of Group of Seven finance ministers and central bankers in Washington at the weekend.
